timeline.title: The aether in two hundred and fifty years
timeline.mini: From Huygens' wave of 1690 to the optical cavities of 2015: the ideas about a medium for light, and the experiments that tested them. Null results in amber, results that fit a moving Earth in blue.
timeline.text: Light was understood as a wave from Huygens (1690) and Young (1804); Fresnel made it a sideways wave in a still, invisible medium, the aether; Maxwell (1862) found that light is an electromagnetic wave whose speed comes from two bench constants. Every experiment then tried to catch the Earth moving through that medium: some fitted a moving Earth (Bradley's aberration, Fizeau's flowing water), others gave null results (Arago, Airy, Michelson–Morley). FitzGerald and Lorentz saved the aether with a contraction; Einstein (1905) showed it was not needed. Sagnac (1913) and Michelson–Gale (1925) found that a loop of light does feel rotation; Miller's claimed wind turned out to follow the temperature; today's cavities find no wind to one part in 10¹⁸ [1]. None of these experiments looks at the shape of the Earth.
maxwell.title: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and its speed comes from a bench
maxwell.mini: Two constants measured with coils and charged plates, μ₀ and ε₀, give the speed of electric and magnetic waves: 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = {{cMax}} km/s, the speed of light. Maxwell, 1862.
maxwell.text: μ₀ says how strongly two currents attract, ε₀ how strongly two charges attract; both come from bench experiments that have nothing to do with light. Maxwell found in 1862 that waves of electric and magnetic field must travel at 1/√(μ₀ε₀). From Weber and Kohlrausch's electrical measurements he got 310,740 km/s, against Fizeau's 314,858 km/s for light [2]: light is an electromagnetic wave. With today's constants the formula gives {{cMax}} km/s. Light had been known as a wave since Huygens and Young, and Fresnel had shown it shakes sideways [1]. A wave seemed to need something to wave in, the aether, and the speed c seemed to be the speed relative to it: if the Earth moved through it, light should go faster one way than the other.
aberr.title: Aberration: a telescope must lean into the starlight
aberr.mini: Starlight falls on a moving telescope like rain on a walker: it must be tipped forward by α, tan α = v/c. For the Earth's 29.78 km/s, α = {{aberr}}″. Bradley found it in 1727.
aberr.text: Bradley watched γ Draconis cross the zenith from 1725 to 1728 and found it swinging by about 20″ over the year, three months out of step with parallax and by the same angle for every star in that part of the sky [1]. The explanation is the telescope's own speed: while the light falls down the tube, the tube moves sideways, so it must lean forward by α, with tan α = v/c, as a walker tips an umbrella into vertical rain. Pointed straight at the star, the back wall catches the light before it reaches the eye. With v = 29.78 km/s, α = {{aberr}}″. The angle depends on the observer's velocity, not on the star's, which is why it is the same for near and far stars. In the animation the Earth's speed is drawn 3,500 times too large.
aberr.verdict: Would favour an Earth at rest: no yearly swing common to all stars, or one that depends on each star's distance.
drag.title: Moving water drags light, by a precise fraction
drag.mini: Fresnel guessed in 1818 that transparent matter carries light along with a fraction 1 − 1/n² of its speed: {{fF}} for water. Fizeau measured it in flowing water in 1851.
drag.text: Arago found in 1810 that a prism bends starlight by the same amount whatever the Earth's motion. Fresnel answered in 1818 that the aether stays still but a transparent body carries light along with a fraction f = 1 − 1/n² of its own speed, n being its refractive index: nothing for air, {{fF}} for water [1]. In 1851 Fizeau sent two beams of light through water flowing in opposite directions and compared them by interference [2]: with the water at about 7.06 m/s, the light gained {{fizDrag}} m/s, not the full {{fizFull}} m/s. At the time this was the best evidence for a still aether and a moving Earth. Relativity later gave the same formula with no aether at all.
airy.title: “Airy's failure” was Fresnel's prediction
airy.mini: Fill a telescope with water and, light being slower, the aberration should grow, said Boscovich. Airy found it unchanged in 1871. Fresnel had predicted exactly that for a moving Earth, in 1818.
airy.text: Flat-earth and geocentric videos call it “Airy's failure”: Airy filled a zenith telescope with water in 1871, watched γ Draconis, and found the same aberration as with air [2], so, they say, the stars move and not the Earth. But Fresnel had predicted this null result 53 years earlier for a moving Earth [1][3]. Inside the water two angles must agree: the ray, bent by refraction to α/n, and the direction the moving tube needs, (v − f v)/(c/n) = v/(nc), also α/n with Fresnel's coefficient. They agree, so the water changes nothing: {{airyIn}}″ inside for n = {{airyN}}. Without the dragging they would differ by {{airyGap}}″, which Airy would have seen. The experiment says nothing about the shape of the ground.
airy.verdict: Would have favoured an Earth at rest in a still aether: a change of the aberration with water, against Fresnel's coefficient measured by Fizeau.
mm.title: Michelson–Morley: two arms, no aether wind
mm.mini: Light sent along and across the Earth's motion through the aether should come back at different times, worth 0.4 of a fringe in 1887. Michelson and Morley saw less than a fortieth of that.
mm.text: A beam is split in two; the halves go along two perpendicular arms of length L to mirrors and back, and are recombined. If the Earth moved through a still aether at v, the arm along the motion would be like swimming upstream and back: (2L/c)/(1 − v²/c²), longer than the arm across, (2L/c)/√(1 − v²/c²). In 1887 the light path was folded to 11 m; with v = 30 km/s, v²/c² = {{mmBeta2}} × 10⁻⁸ and the delay {{mmDt}} × 10⁻¹⁵ s. Turning the instrument by 90° swaps the arms: the fringes should move by {{mmN}} of a fringe. Michelson and Morley saw less than a fortieth of it [1]. A motionless Earth would explain this, but then nothing explains aberration, which needs a relative motion of 30 km/s; and the arms would give the same null result on a disc. In the animation the wind is drawn at half the speed of light.
mm.verdict: Would have shown a still aether with a moving Earth: a fringe shift of about 0.4, turning with the instrument and changing over the day and the year.
contract.title: Lorentz contraction: invented to save the aether, then measured
contract.mini: Shorten the arm along the motion by √(1 − v²/c²) and both round trips take the same time: no fringe moves. FitzGerald (1889) and Lorentz (1892) proposed it ad hoc; later experiments measured its consequences.
contract.text: To keep the aether after 1887, FitzGerald and Lorentz proposed that a body moving through it shrinks along its motion by exactly √(1 − v²/c²) [1]: then t∥ = t⊥ at any speed and no fringe moves. For 30 km/s the shortening is 5 parts in a billion, and no ruler can see it because the ruler shrinks too. It was ad hoc at first. Lorentz then added a “local time” and, in 1904, the full transformations, which Poincaré showed form a group. What changed its status were experiments it was not designed for: Kennedy and Thorndike (1932) with arms of unequal length, Ives and Stilwell (1938) with moving ions, muons in a storage ring, flown atomic clocks. The drawing exaggerates the shortening about 60 million times.
clock.title: A moving clock ticks slower: the light clock
clock.mini: A pulse of light bouncing between two mirrors is a clock. Passing at 0.6 c, its light runs a longer zigzag at the same speed c, so each tick lasts γ = 1.25 times longer: 10 ticks against 8.
clock.text: Einstein (1905) started from two rules: physics is the same in every uniformly moving frame, and light in vacuum always goes at c [1]. Take a clock whose tick is a round trip of light between two mirrors. Seen from a frame where it moves at v, the light runs along a longer zigzag, still at c, so each tick lasts longer: Δt = γ Δτ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). At 0.6 c, γ = 1.25: ten ticks of the clock at rest, eight of the moving one. For the Earth's orbital speed, γ − 1 is only {{gam30}} × 10⁻⁹. It is measured: muons at γ = 29.33 lived {{muMeas}} µs in CERN's storage ring against {{muPred}} µs predicted [2], and atomic clocks flown round the world gained and lost what was predicted [3].
clock.verdict: Would have supported an absolute time: fast muons living 2.2 µs like slow ones, or flown clocks agreeing with clocks on the ground.
vadd.title: Velocities do not simply add, and Fresnel's coefficient falls out
vadd.mini: Einstein's sum, (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²), never passes c. Put in light in water, u′ = c/n, and it gives Fresnel's coefficient 1 − 1/n² with no aether, as von Laue showed in 1907.
vadd.text: In special relativity a speed u′ measured in a frame that moves at v becomes u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²) [1]. At everyday speeds the denominator is 1 and the speeds simply add; near c the sum bends and never passes c (the graph: u′ = c/2). Put in light in water, u′ = c/n: to first order the result is c/n + v(1 − 1/n²), Fresnel's coefficient exactly, as von Laue showed in 1907 [2]. Fizeau's flowing water [3] and Airy's water-filled telescope, once the best evidence for a still aether, are consequences of relativity with no aether at all.
gps.title: GPS clocks run 38 µs a day fast
gps.mini: A GPS satellite's speed slows its clock by {{gpsVel}} µs a day; the weaker gravity up there speeds it up by {{gpsGrav}}. Net +{{gpsNet}} µs a day, 11 km of range: the clocks are tuned slow before launch.
gps.text: A GPS satellite circles at {{gpsV}} km/s, 26,560 km from the Earth's centre. Its speed makes its clock run slow by {{gpsVel}} µs a day (special relativity, −v²/2c²); the weaker gravity at that height makes it run fast by {{gpsGrav}} µs a day (general relativity, GM(1/R − 1/r)/c²). The net drift, +{{gpsNet}} µs a day, would amount to about 11 km of range error a day at the speed of light. The satellite clocks are therefore set slow before launch so that, in orbit, they keep time with clocks on the ground [1]. The relativity that came out of the aether experiments is checked every time a phone finds its position.
sagnac.title: Sagnac and Michelson–Gale: light feels the Earth turn
sagnac.mini: Two beams round a turning loop come back apart by 4AΩ/c². In 1925 a 2010 × 1113 ft rectangle of pipes in Illinois measured 0.230 fringe; the Earth's sidereal rotation gives {{mgpN}}.
sagnac.text: Uniform motion cannot be felt from inside; rotation can. Send two pulses round a closed loop in opposite directions: if the loop turns, the splitter moves on while they travel, and the pulse going with the turn comes back late, by Δt = 4AΩ/c², A being the area enclosed. Sagnac measured it on a turntable in 1913 and called it a proof of the aether, but von Laue had derived it from special relativity in 1911 [1]: it measures rotation, not a medium. In 1925 Michelson, Gale and Pearson laid a rectangle of pipes 2010 × 1113 feet at Clearing, Illinois, pumped the air out and sent light both ways: 0.230 ± 0.005 fringe, against {{mgpN}} for the Earth's sidereal rotation at that latitude, Ω sin φ [2]. Ring lasers a few metres across now read it continuously [3]. In the animation the rim turns at a quarter of the speed of light.
sagnac.verdict: Would favour an Earth that does not turn: a loop at rest on the ground reading zero, or a rate following the Sun (24 h) rather than the stars (23 h 56 min).
bounds.title: The aether wind, ruled out to one part in 10¹⁸
bounds.mini: A 30 km/s aether wind would change the light's round trip by one part in 10⁸. Michelson–Morley ruled it out in 1887; rotating optical cavities now find nothing to one part in 10¹⁸.
bounds.text: The largest difference allowed between the light's round-trip times along two directions, as a fraction of the time, from 1881 to 2015. A wind of 30 km/s would give about 10⁻⁸. Michelson and Morley (1887) saw less than a fortieth of their expected 0.4 fringe [1]; Joos (1930) at most 0.002 fringe where 0.75 was expected [2]; lasers locked to rotating optical cavities reached 10⁻¹⁷ in 2009 and 10⁻¹⁸ in 2015 [3]. Dayton Miller reported a wind of about 9 to 10 km/s in the 1920s, but Shankland and colleagues found in 1955 that his signal followed the temperature of the hut, not the stars [4]. Logarithmic scale: each step is a factor of ten.
bounds.verdict: Would revive the aether: a direction-dependent difference in the speed of light, repeated with independent instruments and following the stars.
earth.title: A change of frame does not change a shape
earth.mini: Einstein and Infeld: Ptolemy's and Copernicus' frames can be used “with equal justification”. True for computing, and it changes velocities, not shapes: seen from the Sun, the Earth is {{earthCm}} cm shorter along its motion.
earth.text: Einstein and Infeld wrote in 1938 that if physics holds in every coordinate system, the struggle between Ptolemy and Copernicus becomes meaningless: “either CS could be used with equal justification” [1]. Videos read this as “the moving Earth is a choice”. It means one may compute in a frame where the Earth stands still; that frame then carries centrifugal and Coriolis terms, and pendulums, gyroscopes, the equatorial bulge and satellites come out exactly as in the other. A distance between two points on the ground, measured with instruments resting on the ground, is the same in every frame. The one change relativity makes is the Earth's length along its motion as described from the Sun's frame: 12,742 km at 30 km/s gives {{earthCm}} cm, five billionths of the diameter, the same for a disc. No choice of coordinates makes a ball flat or a disc round.
